title: What Sorority Rush and Male Influencer Culture Reveal About Young People Today
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: The piece argues that two seemingly unrelated viral phenomena, Bama Rush livestreams of sorority recruitment and manosphere influencer content aimed at young men, are actually symptoms of the same underlying cultural failure: the collapse of what the author calls 'formation institutions' (churches, extended family, mentoring relationships, civic organizations) that used to shape character through slow, repeated, unglamorous contact. He argues Bama Rush is fundamentally about performing belonging publicly because belonging has become scarce, while the manosphere sells status and control by first convincing young men they've been cheated out of both, and that both scripts fill a narrative vacuum left by institutions that no longer tell young people what belonging or manhood are for. The author's central claim is that both audiences are missing the same thing beneath very different content: adults who have committed to knowing them over time and are positioned to challenge their self-conception, something an algorithm-driven comment section or anonymous audience cannot do. He closes by noting that formation cannot be livestreamed because its substance is 'boring, faithful showing-up that never trends,' which is exactly why it is disappearing and being replaced by these viral substitutes.
points: Connects Bama Rush livestreams and manosphere influencer content as parallel symptoms of the same cause: the collapse of 'formation institutions' that used to shape character through slow, repeated, unglamorous contact.

Argues Bama Rush is fundamentally about performing belonging publicly because belonging itself has become scarce, while the manosphere sells status and control by first convincing young men they've been cheated out of both.

Identifies the common deficit beneath both phenomena as the absence of adults committed to knowing young people over time and positioned to challenge their self-conception -- something an anonymous audience or algorithmic comment section cannot replicate.

Closes on the claim that formation 'cannot be livestreamed' because its substance is unglamorous repeated presence rather than performance, which is precisely why it is disappearing and being replaced by viral substitutes.
quotes: These look like unrelated phenomena. I don't think they are. Both are symptoms of the same underlying condition, a generation that has been handed extraordinary tools for self-presentation and almost no formation in how to become a self worth presenting.
Bama Rush is not really about sororities. It is about belonging, performed publicly, in an economy where belonging itself has become scarce and therefore valuable content.
Where Bama Rush sells belonging, the manosphere sells status and control, and it does so by first convincing young men that they have been cheated out of both.
A young man does not need a mentor to challenge his account of himself; he needs a comment section that agrees with him, and the algorithm is very good at finding him one.

What both groups are missing, underneath the very different content, is the same thing: adults who have committed to knowing them over time, who are positioned to say, gently or bluntly, that's not actually who you are, or that's not actually what manhood requires.
Formation is slow, repeated, and unglamorous in a way that content never is. It cannot be livestreamed because most of what it consists of is the boring, faithful showing-up that never trends.
